Chapter 3: The Body’s Wisdom and the Limits of Talk
Most of us grow up believing that if something hurts, the best thing to do is talk it out — to analyze the problem, find a solution, and move on. But...what if some wounds run deeper than words?
Have you ever noticed how your body seems to remember things your mind has long forgotten? Maybe it’s a sudden loud noise, a harsh word, or just a certain look from someone — and out of nowhere, you’re flooded with feelings. Your body reacts before your brain even realizes what’s happening.
Imagine a man who sees himself as totally rational. He’s convinced that if he just understands his feelings, he’ll be able to control them. But then, he gets pulled over by the police. Suddenly, his hands are shaking, his heart’s pounding, and his mind goes completely blank. Later, he feels embarrassed. He tells himself to calm down, to be reasonable. But that fear lingers...and he can’t quite put his finger on why.
That’s the body’s wisdom kicking in. Our nervous system is built to keep us safe. When it senses danger — whether it’s real or just a memory — it gets us ready to fight, to flee, or to freeze. These reactions are automatic, shaped by all the experiences we’ve had, and even by those passed down through our families.
For people who face racism or live with constant threat, the body becomes extra alert. It learns to react quickly, to always expect the worst.
Now, don’t get me wrong — talking about trauma can help. Words can explain what happened. But sometimes, words just aren’t enough to heal. The body needs to feel safe before it can even start letting go of old pain. That’s why so many people struggle to change, even when they really want to. The mind might say, “You’re fine,” but the body’s whispering, “I’m not so sure.”
So, what does healing actually look like? It means learning how to listen to your body — tuning in to its signals, and responding with kindness. Simple things can make a difference: deep, steady breathing...gentle movement...even a mindful touch. These aren’t magic solutions. But they’re a place to start. Little by little, they help your nervous system find new ways to handle stress.
Take the story of a woman who spent years in talk therapy. Her anxiety never really shifted until she started paying close attention to her body. She noticed when her shoulders tensed up, when her breath turned shallow, or when her jaw tightened. Instead of brushing off those signals, she learned to pause...breathe...and let her body know it was safe. Slowly, the anxiety loosened its grip. Hard days still came, but she no longer felt trapped by her own reactions.
Most people underestimate the power of these small changes. They’re hoping for quick fixes and dramatic turnarounds. But real healing is slow — it’s built on tiny moments of awareness and care. It’s not about wiping away the past, but about learning how to live with it in a new, gentler way.
This approach is especially powerful for folks carrying racialized trauma. See, the body’s responses aren’t just personal. They’re shaped by history, by family, and by community. Healing, then, isn’t just about what you do on your own. It’s about finding — or even creating — spaces where you feel safe. Where your body can finally relax. Where old wounds can start to mend.
This work doesn’t have an endpoint. There will always be setbacks, moments of fear or pain. But every small act of care, every moment when you tune in and respond with compassion — it all adds up. Over time, these little steps create a new sense of safety. A new way of being in the world.
